Native engine book, chapter 4: fixed exogenous variables

Source: vignettes/articles/native-book-4-fixed-x.qmd

In a mediation model the treatment and the covariates are exogenous: nothing in the model explains them. Their means, variances and covariances are parameters of the joint model, and they carry no information about the paths. The fixed_x argument of fit_sem() stops estimating them and holds them at their sample values, as lavaan’s fixed.x = TRUE does. This chapter shows exactly what that changes (the parameter count and the likelihood) and what it does not (the estimates and standard errors of the structural parameters, that is the paths, the residual variances and the intercepts of the other variables; the degrees of freedom; and the chi-square), proves why, and shows which comparisons the engine then refuses. The engine is experimental.

You need Chapters 1 to 3 (the RAM matrices, the discrepancy, the moment count) and the multivariate normal density
You get the moments fixed_x fixes and where they go in the RAM matrices, the factorization argument for equal structural estimates and standard errors (and what changes when only some exogenous variables are fixed), the conditional log likelihood derived and computed by hand, its parameter count, and the refusals with their messages
Time about 45 minutes 
library(medfit)

Attaching package: 'medfit'
The following object is masked from 'package:stats':

    decompose
library(generics)

Attaching package: 'generics'
The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    as.difftime, as.factor, as.ordered, intersect, is.element, setdiff,
    setequal, union
rd <- function(x, d = 4) round(x, d)
d <- mediation_demo
n <- nrow(d)

# Two exogenous variables (treatment and covariate1) and two outcomes (mediator1 and outcome)
full <- "
  mediator1 ~ a * treatment + covariate1
  outcome ~ b * mediator1 + cp * treatment + covariate1
"
restricted <- paste0(full, "cp == 0\n")   # one restriction, so that df = 1 and the chi-square is not zero

1. Which moments are fixed

A variable is exogenous here if it appears only as a predictor, never as the target of a path (treatment and covariate1). With fixed_x = TRUE every such variable is selected; a character vector selects a subset. The selected variables’ means, variances and the covariances among the exogenous variables that involve a selected one become fixed moments: the engine gives them the sample values (divisor \(n\), so \(S_{ff} = \frac1n\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(x_i - \bar x)^\top\), the matrix of Chapter 1) and no longer treats them as parameters.

fx <- fit_sem(full, d, meanstructure = TRUE, fixed_x = TRUE, information = "expected")
fx@internals$fixed_x
[1] "treatment"  "covariate1"
tidy(fx)[, c("term", "estimate", "std_error", "fixed_x")]
# A tibble: 14 × 4
   term                   estimate std_error fixed_x
   <chr>                     <dbl>     <dbl> <lgl>
 1 a                        0.581     0.0986 FALSE
 2 mediator1~covariate1     0.448     0.0483 FALSE
 3 b                        0.573     0.0531 FALSE
 4 cp                       0.204     0.109  FALSE
 5 outcome~covariate1       0.356     0.0565 FALSE
 6 mediator1~~mediator1     0.954     0.0674 FALSE
 7 outcome~~outcome         1.07      0.0759 FALSE
 8 mediator1~1              0.0844    0.0696 FALSE
 9 outcome~1                0.197     0.0740 FALSE
10 treatment~~treatment     0.250    NA      TRUE
11 treatment~~covariate1   -0.0700   NA      TRUE
12 covariate1~~covariate1   1.04     NA      TRUE
13 treatment~1              0.502    NA      TRUE
14 covariate1~1             0.0174   NA      TRUE

The last five rows are the fixed moments (the variances and covariance of the two exogenous variables, and, because this fit has a mean structure, their two means). They are flagged fixed_x = TRUE and have no standard error, because they are no longer estimates; the engine keeps them in its parameter table (fx@table). Check that they are the sample moments:

exo <- c("treatment", "covariate1")
xm <- as.matrix(d[, exo])
s_ff <- cov(xm) * (n - 1) / n
tab <- fx@table
fixed_tab <- tab[tab$fixed_x, c("lhs", "op", "rhs", "est")]
fixed_tab$sample_value <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(fixed_tab)), function(i) {
  row <- fixed_tab[i, ]
  if (row$op == "~1") colMeans(xm)[[row$lhs]] else s_ff[row$lhs, row$rhs]
}, numeric(1))
c(largest_difference = max(abs(fixed_tab$est - fixed_tab$sample_value)))
largest_difference
      8.326673e-16 
fixed_tab[, c("est", "sample_value")] <- rd(fixed_tab[, c("est", "sample_value")], 6)
fixed_tab
          lhs op        rhs       est sample_value
8   treatment ~~  treatment  0.249994     0.249994
9   treatment ~~ covariate1 -0.069969    -0.069969
10 covariate1 ~~ covariate1  1.039839     1.039839
12  treatment ~1             0.502500     0.502500
13 covariate1 ~1             0.017352     0.017352

In the RAM matrices of Chapter 1 these entries of \(S_{\text{ram}}\) and \(m\) become constants, in the same place a fixed value such as y ~ 0.5*x would sit; the parameter vector no longer has a slot for them.

2. Parameters, moments and degrees of freedom

Counting moments (Chapter 1): \(p(p+1)/2\) distinct variances and covariances, plus \(p\) means with a mean structure. With \(k\) fixed variables, the fixed moments are removed from the count of moments (the engine does not ask the model to explain them) as well as from the count of parameters. Each removal is the same size, so the difference, the degrees of freedom, does not change. Four fits to the restricted model:

fits <- list(
  free_cov = fit_sem(restricted, d),
  fixed_cov = fit_sem(restricted, d, fixed_x = TRUE),
  free_mean = fit_sem(restricted, d, meanstructure = TRUE),
  fixed_mean = fit_sem(restricted, d, meanstructure = TRUE, fixed_x = TRUE)
)
data.frame(
  fit = names(fits),
  parameters = vapply(fits, function(f) length(f@theta), numeric(1)),
  equality_rank = vapply(fits, function(f) f@internals$eq_rank, numeric(1)),
  fixed_moments = vapply(fits, function(f) f@internals$ram$n_fixed_x, numeric(1)),
  moments = vapply(fits, function(f) medfit:::.sem_moments(f@internals$ram), numeric(1)),
  df = vapply(fits, function(f) f@df, numeric(1)),
  chisq = vapply(fits, function(f) round(f@n_obs * f@f, 6), numeric(1)),
  row.names = NULL
)
         fit parameters equality_rank fixed_moments moments df    chisq
1   free_cov         10             1             0      10  1 3.491141
2  fixed_cov          7             1             3       7  1 3.491141
3  free_mean         14             1             0      14  1 3.491141
4 fixed_mean          9             1             5       9  1 3.491141

With three variances and covariances fixed (covariance structure) the parameter count falls by 3 and the moment count by 3; with the two means added it falls by 5 and 5. The degrees of freedom (1, from the one restriction cp == 0) and the chi-square are identical in all four.

3. Why the estimates and standard errors do not change

This section proves the claim in the title for fixed_x = TRUE, checks it, and then shows what changes when only some exogenous variables are fixed.

Setup. Take fixed_x = TRUE, so that \(x\), the vector of the \(k\) fixed variables, holds every exogenous variable, and let \(y\) be the vector of all other observed variables. No error of \(y\) is correlated with \(x\): such a covariance would be a statement about a fixed variable, which the engine refuses (Section 5). In the RAM form, a variable with no incoming path is its own error plus its intercept: \(x = m_x + e_x\). So \(x \sim N(\mu_x, \Sigma_{xx})\) with \(\mu_x = m_x\) and \(\Sigma_{xx} = S_{\text{ram},xx}\), and nothing in the model touches these. Given \(x\), the rest of the model is linear: \(y = (I - A_{y y})^{-1}(m_y + A_{y x}\,x + e_y)\), so

\[ y \mid x \;\sim\; N\bigl(c + \Gamma x,\; \Psi\bigr), \qquad \Gamma = (I - A_{y y})^{-1} A_{y x}, \quad c = (I - A_{y y})^{-1} m_y, \quad \Psi = (I - A_{y y})^{-1} S_{y y} (I - A_{y y})^{-\top}. \]

Here \(A_{y y}\) and \(A_{y x}\) are the blocks of \(A\), \(S_{y y}\) is the error covariance of \(y\), and \(c\), \(\Gamma\) and \(\Psi\) depend only on the structural parameters \(\psi\) (the paths, the residual variances, the intercepts of \(y\)) and not on \(\eta = (\mu_x, \Sigma_{xx})\).

Step 1: factor the density. For each row, \(f(x_i, y_i) = f(y_i \mid x_i;\, \psi)\; f(x_i;\, \eta)\), the definition of a conditional density. Taking logs and summing over rows,

\[ \ell(\psi, \eta) = \ell_c(\psi) + \ell_m(\eta), \]

where \(\ell_c\) is the conditional log likelihood of \(y\) given \(x\) and \(\ell_m\) the marginal one of \(x\). The two parts have no parameter in common: this identity holds for every value of \((\psi, \eta)\).

Step 2: maximize. Because \(\ell\) is a sum of a function of \(\psi\) and a function of \(\eta\), it is maximized by maximizing each separately. The maximizer of \(\ell_m\) is the sample mean and the divisor-\(n\) covariance matrix of \(x\) (the standard result for the normal distribution). The maximizer \(\hat\psi\) of \(\ell_c\) does not involve \(\eta\) at all. So the free fit’s structural estimates are \(\hat\psi\). The fixed fit holds \(\eta\) at \(\hat\eta\) and maximizes the same \(\ell\) over \(\psi\), which is \(\ell_c(\psi)\) plus a constant: the same \(\hat\psi\).

Step 3: the information. The cross second derivatives \(\partial^2\ell/\partial\psi\,\partial\eta^\top\) are zero, because \(\partial\ell/\partial\psi = \partial\ell_c/\partial\psi\) does not depend on \(\eta\). The information matrix is therefore block diagonal, and its \(\psi\) block is the information of \(\ell_c\) alone. The covariance of \(\hat\psi\) is the inverse of that block, the same whether or not the \(\eta\) block is present. So the standard errors of the structural estimates agree between the two fits. The minimized discrepancy is the same too: the fixed fit’s discrepancy is the free discrepancy of Chapter 1 with \(\eta\) set to \(\hat\eta\), and the free optimum has \(\eta = \hat\eta\) by Step 2, so the two minima are the value of one function at one point. Hence the chi-square agrees.

Now check each step on our data. The estimates and standard errors of the structural parameters:

free <- fit_sem(full, d, meanstructure = TRUE, information = "expected")
shared <- intersect(names(free@theta), names(fx@theta))
c(estimates = max(abs(free@theta[shared] - fx@theta[shared])),
  standard_errors = max(abs(sqrt(diag(free@vcov))[shared] - sqrt(diag(fx@vcov))[shared])))
      estimates standard_errors
   4.440892e-16    2.498002e-16

The estimates and standard errors agree to rounding. Step 3 is the claim that the information has no cross block; look at the free fit’s information between the fixed moments and the structural parameters, in the engine’s raw coordinates, for both kinds of information:

ram <- free@internals$ram
smp <- medfit:::.sem_sample(free@data, ram)
info_e <- medfit:::.sem_info_expected(free@theta, ram, smp, NULL)
info_o <- medfit:::.sem_info_observed(free@theta, ram, smp, NULL)
moment_names <- c("treatment~~treatment", "treatment~~covariate1", "covariate1~~covariate1",
                  "treatment~1", "covariate1~1")
structural <- setdiff(rownames(info_e), moment_names)
cross <- function(m) max(abs(m[moment_names, structural]))
cross_table <- data.frame(
  information = c("expected", "observed"),
  cross_block_largest_entry = c(cross(info_e), cross(info_o)),
  largest_entry_of_the_matrix = c(max(abs(info_e)), max(abs(info_o)))
)
cross_table$orders_of_magnitude_below <- round(log10(cross_table$largest_entry_of_the_matrix /
                                                       cross_table$cross_block_largest_entry), 1)
cross_table
  information cross_block_largest_entry largest_entry_of_the_matrix
1    expected              1.011261e-13                    3324.189
2    observed              9.436680e-09                    3324.189
  orders_of_magnitude_below
1                      16.5
2                      11.5

The cross block has 5 \(\times\) 9 entries. Its largest entry is 16.5 orders of magnitude below the largest entry of the matrix for the expected information and 11.5 for the observed one (which the engine computes by finite differences of the gradient, so it carries a numerical error that the expected one does not). Both are zero to numerical precision, as Step 3 says.

Fixing a subset

With fixed_x = "treatment", only the moments that involve treatment are fixed: its mean, its variance and its covariance with covariate1. The variance and the mean of covariate1 stay free. The structural parameters keep their estimates and standard errors; the free moments of covariate1 keep their estimates but not their standard errors:

subset_fit <- fit_sem(full, d, meanstructure = TRUE, fixed_x = "treatment", information = "expected")
both <- intersect(names(free@theta), names(subset_fit@theta))
own_moments <- c("covariate1~~covariate1", "covariate1~1")
se_change <- sqrt(diag(subset_fit@vcov))[both] - sqrt(diag(free@vcov))[both]
c(structural_estimates = max(abs(subset_fit@theta[structural] - free@theta[structural])),
  structural_standard_errors = max(abs(se_change[structural])),
  covariate1_moment_estimates = max(abs(subset_fit@theta[own_moments] - free@theta[own_moments])))
       structural_estimates  structural_standard_errors
               6.661338e-16                2.081668e-16
covariate1_moment_estimates
               2.220446e-16 
signif(se_change[own_moments], 3)
covariate1~~covariate1           covariate1~1
             -0.001380              -0.000482

The reason is the information of the exogenous block itself. In the free fit the standard error of a free moment \(j\) is \(\sqrt{(I^{-1})_{j j}}\) over the whole exogenous block, and that block is not diagonal. Under normality the means and the (co)variances share no information (Chapter 1, Section 8), but within the means \(\Sigma^{-1}\) couples the mean of covariate1 with the mean of treatment, and within the (co)variances the variance of covariate1 shares information with the variance of treatment and with their covariance. Fixing the moments of treatment removes those partners, so the standard errors of covariate1’s moments come from a smaller block. For the mean this has a closed form. With \(s_{11}\), \(s_{12}\), \(s_{22}\) the entries of \(S_{ff}\) (1 for treatment, 2 for covariate1), the free fit’s standard error is \(\sqrt{s_{22}/n}\) and the subset fit’s is \(\sqrt{(s_{22} - s_{12}^2/s_{11})/n}\), the conditional variance of covariate1 given treatment, over \(n\):

se_mean <- function(f) sqrt(diag(f@vcov))[["covariate1~1"]]
c(free_fit = se_mean(free), by_hand_free = sqrt(s_ff[2, 2] / n),
  subset_fit = se_mean(subset_fit), by_hand_subset = sqrt((s_ff[2, 2] - s_ff[1, 2]^2 / s_ff[1, 1]) / n))
      free_fit   by_hand_free     subset_fit by_hand_subset
    0.05098626     0.05098626     0.05050386     0.05050386

The structural block still has no cross term with any exogenous moment, so Step 3 holds for it unchanged.

4. The conditional log likelihood

logLik() for the fixed fit is the conditional log likelihood \(\ell_c(\hat\psi)\). From Step 1, \(\ell_c = \ell - \ell_m(\eta)\), so at the estimates

\[ \ell_c(\hat\psi) = \ell(\hat\psi, \hat\eta) - \ell_m(\hat\eta) . \]

The marginal term. Evaluate \(\ell_m\) at the sample moments. Each row contributes \(-\tfrac12\bigl[k\log 2\pi + \log|S_{ff}| + (x_i - \bar x)^\top S_{ff}^{-1}(x_i - \bar x)\bigr]\). By the trace argument of Chapter 1 (Step 3), \(\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^\top S_{ff}^{-1}(x_i - \bar x) = n\operatorname{tr}(S_{ff}^{-1} S_{ff}) = n k\). So

\[ \ell_m(\hat\eta) = -\frac n2 \bigl(\log|S_{ff}| + k + k\log 2\pi\bigr), \qquad \ell_c(\hat\psi) = \ell(\hat\psi, \hat\eta) + \frac n2 \bigl(\log|S_{ff}| + k + k\log 2\pi\bigr). \]

This is the correction logLik() applies to the joint value. Check it three ways: against the joint value from the free fit, against a direct computation of the conditional density from the RAM matrices, and against lavaan.

k <- length(exo)
marginal <- -0.5 * n * (as.numeric(determinant(s_ff, logarithm = TRUE)$modulus) + k + k * log(2 * pi))
c(joint_logLik_free_fit = as.numeric(logLik(free)),
  conditional_logLik_fixed_fit = as.numeric(logLik(fx)),
  difference_of_the_two = as.numeric(logLik(fx)) - as.numeric(logLik(free)),
  minus_marginal_term = -marginal)
       joint_logLik_free_fit conditional_logLik_fixed_fit
                  -2001.8256                   -1139.9279
       difference_of_the_two          minus_marginal_term
                    861.8977                     861.8977

By hand from the conditional model of the setup: the endogenous block is mediator1 and outcome, the mean of each row given its fixed variables is \(c + \Gamma x_i\) and the covariance is \(\Psi\). Sum the bivariate normal log densities:

mats <- medfit:::.sem_ram_mats(fx@internals$ram, fx@theta)
A <- mats$a
s_ram <- mats$s
m <- medfit:::.sem_ram_m(fx@internals$ram, fx@theta)
vars <- fx@internals$ram$vars
endo <- c("mediator1", "outcome")
iy <- match(endo, vars)
ix <- match(exo, vars)
b_yy <- solve(diag(length(endo)) - A[iy, iy])
Psi <- b_yy %*% s_ram[iy, iy] %*% t(b_yy)
data_mat <- as.matrix(d[, c(endo, exo)])
ll_by_hand <- sum(vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
  mu_i <- drop(b_yy %*% (m[iy] + A[iy, ix] %*% data_mat[i, exo]))
  e <- data_mat[i, endo] - mu_i
  -0.5 * (length(endo) * log(2 * pi) + log(det(Psi)) + drop(t(e) %*% solve(Psi) %*% e))
}, numeric(1)))
c(by_hand = ll_by_hand, logLik = as.numeric(logLik(fx)))
  by_hand    logLik
-1139.928 -1139.928

The parameter count. logLik() also carries a df attribute, the parameter count behind AIC and BIC. With a mean structure the free intercepts are in the parameter vector already. Without one, the likelihood still has means: the model’s means are saturated, one free mean for each variable that is not fixed (a fixed variable’s mean is a constant, not a parameter). So the count is

\[ \text{df}_{\text{logLik}} = (q - \text{rank}) + (p - k)\,\mathbb 1[\text{no mean structure}] , \]

with \(q - \text{rank}\) the free parameters after equality constraints. Check against the four fits of Section 2, and compare with lavaan, which reports the same count for the mean-structure fit:

ll <- lapply(fits, logLik)
data.frame(
  fit = names(fits),
  logLik = vapply(ll, as.numeric, numeric(1)),
  df_attribute = vapply(ll, attr, numeric(1), "df"),
  formula = vapply(fits, function(f) {
    p <- length(f@internals$ram$obs)
    kk <- length(f@internals$fixed_x)
    (length(f@theta) - f@internals$eq_rank) + (p - kk) * !isTRUE(f@internals$ram$has_mean)
  }, numeric(1)),
  AIC = vapply(fits, AIC, numeric(1)),
  BIC = vapply(fits, BIC, numeric(1)),
  row.names = NULL
)
         fit    logLik df_attribute formula      AIC      BIC
1   free_cov -2003.571           13      13 4033.142 4085.031
2  fixed_cov -1141.673            8       8 2299.347 2331.279
3  free_mean -2003.571           13      13 4033.142 4085.031
4 fixed_mean -1141.673            8       8 2299.347 2331.279

The two fixed fits have the same likelihood, parameter count, AIC and BIC whether or not a mean structure is declared, and so do the two free fits: declaring means only moves the intercepts into the parameter vector.

lv_fixed <- lavaan::sem(restricted, d, meanstructure = TRUE, fixed.x = TRUE, information = "expected")
lv_free <- lavaan::sem(restricted, d, meanstructure = TRUE, fixed.x = FALSE, information = "expected")
lv_row <- function(f) {
  unname(c(lavaan::fitMeasures(f, "logl"), lavaan::fitMeasures(f, "npar"), lavaan::fitMeasures(f, "chisq"),
           lavaan::fitMeasures(f, "df"), lavaan::fitMeasures(f, "aic"), lavaan::fitMeasures(f, "bic")))
}
mf_row <- function(f) {
  unname(c(as.numeric(logLik(f)), attr(logLik(f), "df"), f@n_obs * f@f, f@df, AIC(f), BIC(f)))
}
data.frame(
  quantity = c("logLik", "df of logLik (lavaan: npar)", "chisq", "df", "AIC", "BIC"),
  medfit_fixed = mf_row(fits$fixed_mean),
  lavaan_fixed.x_TRUE = lv_row(lv_fixed),
  medfit_free = mf_row(fits$free_mean),
  lavaan_fixed.x_FALSE = lv_row(lv_free)
)
                     quantity medfit_fixed lavaan_fixed.x_TRUE  medfit_free

(Both standard-error computations use the expected information.)

OpenMx can hold the exogenous moments at their sample values with fixed paths. Its -2 log L is the joint value at those moments, so it equals the free fit’s, and the conditional value differs from it by the marginal term:

suppressMessages(library(OpenMx))
mxOption(NULL, "Number of Threads", 1)
dat <- d[, c("mediator1", "treatment", "covariate1", "outcome")]
mu_s <- colMeans(dat)
s_s <- cov(dat) * (n - 1) / n
mod <- mxModel(
  "fixedx", type = "RAM", manifestVars = names(dat),
  mxPath("treatment", "mediator1", values = 0.4, labels = "a"),
  mxPath("covariate1", "mediator1", values = 0.1, labels = "m_c"),
  mxPath("mediator1", "outcome", values = 0.4, labels = "b"),
  mxPath("covariate1", "outcome", values = 0.1, labels = "y_c"),
  mxPath(c("mediator1", "outcome"), arrows = 2, values = 1, labels = c("vm", "vy")),
  mxPath("treatment", arrows = 2, free = FALSE, values = s_s["treatment", "treatment"]),
  mxPath("covariate1", arrows = 2, free = FALSE, values = s_s["covariate1", "covariate1"]),
  mxPath("treatment", "covariate1", arrows = 2, free = FALSE, values = s_s["treatment", "covariate1"]),
  mxPath("one", c("treatment", "covariate1"), free = FALSE, values = mu_s[c("treatment", "covariate1")]),
  mxPath("one", c("mediator1", "outcome"), values = 0, labels = c("i_m", "i_y")),
  mxData(dat, type = "raw")
)
mx_run <- mxRun(mod, silent = TRUE)
data.frame(
  quantity = c("OpenMx -2 log L (joint, moments held)", "medfit free fit, -2 log L (joint)",
               "medfit fixed fit, -2 log L (conditional)", "conditional + 2 x marginal term"),
  value = c(summary(mx_run)$Minus2LogLikelihood, -2 * as.numeric(logLik(fits$free_mean)),
            -2 * as.numeric(logLik(fits$fixed_mean)), -2 * as.numeric(logLik(fits$fixed_mean)) - 2 * marginal)
)
                                  quantity    value
1    OpenMx -2 log L (joint, moments held) 4007.142
2        medfit free fit, -2 log L (joint) 4007.142
3 medfit fixed fit, -2 log L (conditional) 2283.347
4          conditional + 2 x marginal term 4007.142

(Here cp == 0 is the restriction, written in OpenMx by leaving out the path from treatment to outcome.)

5. What the engine refuses

Because \(\ell_c\) conditions on different variables for different fixed sets, two such values do not measure the same thing. The difference of two of them, or two AIC values, is meaningless, so the engine refuses to produce it. The messages (captured with tryCatch so the page keeps rendering):

say <- function(expr) {
  tryCatch({
    expr
    "no error"
  }, error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
}
fixed_full <- fit_sem(full, d, fixed_x = TRUE)
fixed_restricted <- fit_sem(restricted, d, fixed_x = TRUE)
free_restricted <- fit_sem(restricted, d)
fixed_treatment <- fit_sem(restricted, d, fixed_x = "treatment")
d_other <- d
d_other$outcome <- d_other$outcome + 1
fixed_other_data <- fit_sem(restricted, d_other, fixed_x = TRUE)
msgs <- c(
  `anova, fixed vs free` = say(anova(fixed_restricted, free_restricted)),
  `AIC, fixed vs free` = say(AIC(fixed_restricted, free_restricted)),
  `BIC, free vs fixed` = say(BIC(free_restricted, fixed_restricted)),
  `AIC, different fixed sets` = say(AIC(fixed_restricted, fixed_treatment)),
  `AIC, fixed fit vs an lm` = say(AIC(fixed_restricted, lm(outcome ~ treatment, d))),
  `anova, same set, different data` = say(anova(fixed_full, fixed_other_data)),
  `AIC, same set, different data` = say(AIC(fixed_full, fixed_other_data))
)
cat(sprintf("%s:\n  %s\n", names(msgs), msgs), sep = "\n")
anova, fixed vs free:
  the fits have different `fixed_x` sets (fixed_restricted: covariate1, treatment; free_restricted: none): their likelihoods condition on different variables, so they cannot be compared

AIC, fixed vs free:
  the fits have different `fixed_x` sets (fixed_restricted: covariate1, treatment; free_restricted: none): their likelihoods condition on different variables, so they cannot be compared

BIC, free vs fixed:
  the fits have different `fixed_x` sets (free_restricted: none; fixed_restricted: covariate1, treatment): their likelihoods condition on different variables, so they cannot be compared

AIC, different fixed sets:
  the fits have different `fixed_x` sets (fixed_restricted: covariate1, treatment; fixed_treatment: treatment): their likelihoods condition on different variables, so they cannot be compared

AIC, fixed fit vs an lm:
  a SEMFit with `fixed_x` has a conditional likelihood and cannot be compared with a model of another class: lm(outcome ~ treatment, d)

anova, same set, different data:
  'fixed_full' and 'fixed_other_data' were fitted to different data. With `fixed_x` the likelihood conditions on the data's fixed block.

AIC, same set, different data:
  'fixed_full' and 'fixed_other_data' were fitted to different data. With `fixed_x` the likelihood conditions on the data's fixed block.

Comparisons within one fixed set and one data set are allowed, and they are exactly what the free fits would give:

anova(fixed_full, fixed_restricted)
Likelihood-ratio (chi-square difference) test for SEMFit models

n = 400; Chisq is n times the minimized discrepancy

                 Df  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
fixed_full        0 0.0000
fixed_restricted  1 3.4911     3.4911       1     0.0617 .
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
free_full <- fit_sem(full, d)
anova(free_full, free_restricted)
Likelihood-ratio (chi-square difference) test for SEMFit models

n = 400; Chisq is n times the minimized discrepancy

                Df  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
free_full        0 0.0000
free_restricted  1 3.4911     3.4911       1     0.0617 .
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The two tables are the same test: the chi-square difference of a nested pair does not depend on whether the exogenous moments are fixed.

Two more refusals concern the model itself. A statement about a selected variable’s moments contradicts the request to fix them, and a name that is not exogenous cannot be fixed:

msgs <- c(
  `statement on a fixed variable` = say(fit_sem(paste0(full, "treatment ~~ treatment\n"), d, fixed_x = TRUE)),
  `fixed_x names the outcome` = say(fit_sem(full, d, fixed_x = "outcome"))
)
cat(sprintf("%s:\n  %s\n", names(msgs), msgs), sep = "\n")
statement on a fixed variable:
  `fixed_x` fixes the moments of the selected variables, but the model has a statement on them (treatment ~~ treatment): remove the statement, or leave the variable out of `fixed_x`

fixed_x names the outcome:
  `fixed_x` names variables that are not exogenous observed variables of the model: outcome

Finally, mbco_sem() (the test of an indirect effect of Chapter 5) refits the model text on the data the fit used, with the fit’s fixed_x. The statistic is the same as from the free fit, since the structural estimates and the discrepancy are:

c(from_fixed_fit = unname(mbco_sem(fixed_full, "a", "b")$statistic),
  from_free_fit = unname(mbco_sem(fit_sem(full, d), "a", "b")$statistic))
from_fixed_fit  from_free_fit
      33.35322       33.35322

6. When to use it

Fixing the exogenous moments shrinks the problem: with many covariates the free fit has a parameter for every variance and covariance among them, and the fixed fit has none, so it is smaller. The price is the likelihood: it is conditional, comparable only within one fixed set and one data set, and it is not the joint likelihood a different package may report. When the question is about the paths (their estimates, standard errors, tests) the answer is the same either way, as Section 3 proved; the standard errors of exogenous moments left free next to fixed ones are the exception that section showed. When the question is about information criteria across models, fit them all with the same fixed_x.

Check yourself

  1. In Section 3 where does the proof use that no statement is made about the fixed variables’ moments? (Answer: Step 2 needs no parameter or constraint shared between \(\psi\) and \(\eta\). A constraint linking a moment to a path ties them, and then the structural estimates change. A fixed value such as treatment ~~ 0.25*treatment leaves the structural estimates alone but restricts \(\eta\), so the discrepancy and the chi-square change. The engine refuses both kinds of statement.)
  2. With \(p = 6\) observed variables, \(k = 3\) fixed, no mean structure, and 11 free parameters after constraints, what is the df of logLik()? (Answer: \(11 + (6 - 3) = 14\).)
  3. The fixed and the free fit report different logLik() values for the same model and data. Which is wrong? (Answer: neither: they are different quantities, the conditional and the joint log likelihood, and differ by the marginal term of Section 4.)
